title: Beyond Performance
author: Doug O’Brien and Lucy Gambier
summary: Doug O'Brien and Lucy Gambier recount a Generative Learning professional development session they led at the Ted Wragg Trust's TedFest, designed as a model lesson so participants would experience the cognitive science rather than just hear it. They argue that engagement and visible task success are not evidence of learning, and that teachers should ask what thinking a task requires. The piece walks through schema, Mayer's Select-Organise-Integrate model and cognitive load theory, distinguishing unnecessary cognitive demand from productive effort. It then describes three generative tasks, mapping, drawing and summarising, each sequenced after explicit explanation because generative learning needs knowledge to generate with. The authors tie the ideas to strategies in their Cornwall Education Learning Trust framework, including Harness Attention, Expert Exposition, Faded Scaffolding and Deliberate Practice. They close by urging teachers to make the invisible cognitive processes behind learning the foundation of the visible classroom activity.
points: Busyness, procedural fluency and enthusiastic participation can all coexist with shallow understanding, so task design should start from the thinking required.
Prior knowledge and schema determine task difficulty, so the same task imposes different cognitive demands on different learners.
Cognitive load theory separates unnecessary demands that interfere with learning from productive effort that builds connections.
Mapping, drawing and summarising work as generative strategies only when they follow explicit teaching of the essential knowledge.
Over-scaffolding can strip out the productive struggle needed to encode learning, so support should be responsive and faded.
quotes: There is an important distinction between learners being busy, completing tasks, demonstrating procedural fluency or appearing successful in the moment, and learners developing the knowledge and understanding that will be encoded into long-term memory beyond the lesson.
The critical question becomes not simply what task have we designed?, but what thinking does the task require, and how will that thinking contribute to learning?

A schema can be understood as an organised network of knowledge and concepts held in long-term memory. Rather than storing every piece of information as an isolated fact, our minds develop connections between ideas, experiences and existing understanding.
Attention is not simply about compliance or silence. It is about directing limited cognitive resources towards the knowledge that matters.
We do not want to make learning difficult simply for the sake of difficulty. Nor do we want to remove every challenge in pursuit of smooth, successful task completion.

We did not begin with an unfamiliar concept-mapping task and expect participants to independently construct an understanding of cognitive science. We first introduced and explained the essential knowledge. Only then did we ask colleagues to do something generative with it. Generative learning requires something to generate with.
We often see scaffolding remove both the cognitive demand, and the productive struggle needed to encode into long-term memory.
Our challenge as educators is to ensure that the visible activity in our classrooms is underpinned by the invisible cognitive processes that make learning possible.
context: Learning is defined by durable change in memory, not by in-the-moment performance.
Task design should begin with the thinking a task demands before choosing a strategy.
Schema explains why prior knowledge changes how hard a task is.
Attention is treated as a cognitive resource to direct, not a behavior to police.
Productive struggle differs from needless difficulty, and teachers must tell them apart.
Sequencing matters: explicit knowledge first, generative tasks second.
Excess scaffolding can remove the effort that makes learning stick.
The session's closing claim ties visible classroom activity to invisible cognitive processes.
